The Common rocket frog (Colostethus inguinalis) of Panama exhibits relatively small body sizes typical of its genus. Gravid females attain a maximum recorded wet body mass of 1.55 grams [Wwi = 1.55 grams], which places this species among the smaller Neotropical dendrobatids. At the other end of the life cycle, newly hatched individuals emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably diminutive weight of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a figure derived from the roughly 2 millimeter diameter of the yolk-laden eggs. This substantial size differential between neonate and adult reflects the considerable post-hatching growth required before reproductive maturity can be attained. The eggs, which are deposited in terrestrial leaf litter, are attended by the male parent who maintains hydration until the embryos are ready to hatch. Females typically invest considerable energy into each clutch, producing relatively few, large yolked ova rather than many small ones, a strategy that trades offspring number for per-offspring investment in a competitive understory environment.

Developmental timing in this species has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with eggs hatching approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] aft at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]er oviposition. The resulting tadpoles are then transported on the back of the male parent to small pools or water-filled tree holes where they continue their larval development. The transition from a fully aquatic tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile, marked by tail resorption and the development of lungs, occurs after approximately 35 days  from the ti at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]me of hatching. This relatively brief larval period, lasting just over a month at this temperature, is characteristic of many small stream-breeding dendrobatids that utilize ephemeral aquatic microhabitats. The metamorphosing individuals emerge from the water as fully formed froglets, measuring merely a few millimeters in snout-vent length, ready to commence terrestrial foraging.

Juveniles then enter a period of rapid somatic growth and development that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. Under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], female Common rocket frogs reach puberty approximately 140 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 140 days following metamorphosis]. This developmental delay, spanning nearly five months after the larval-juvenile transition, allows sufficient time for the froglets to achieve the body size necessary for successful reproduction, which in this species involves the production of relatively large, yolk-rich eggs. During this interval, the growing juveniles feed actively on small arthropods such as springtails, mites, and tiny dipterans, steadily accumulating the energy reserves required for later reproductive effort. Field observations indicate that individuals in natural populations may reach maturity slightly later than those in captivity, presumably due to variation in food availability and thermal conditions across their forest floor habitat.

Reproduction in Colostethus inguinalis follows a pattern well documented among Neotropical leaf-litter frogs. Females produce a single clutch at a time, with a maximum fecundity of approximately 0.27 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.27 offspring per day], a rate that translates to roughly one egg every three to four days during the peak breeding season when maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This sustained, low-level reproductive output is typical of frogs that deposit eggs in small, scattered clutches rather than in a single large mass. The maximum clutch frequency and egg production rate have been estimated from captive breeding colonies, where individuals have been observed to reproduce consistently for extended periods given adequate nutrition. The strategy of producing a small number of eggs on a near-daily basis during favorable conditions may allow females to buffer against unpredictable rainfall and fluctuating resource availability in their seasonal tropical environment.

Longevity data for this species, also collected under captive conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], which is comparatively extended for a frog of such diminutive body size. This lifespan likely reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality risk experienced by a chemically defended, diurnal leaf-litter frog, coupled with the species' moderate metabolic demands. Respirometry trials conducted at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have documented a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the low resting metabolism characteristic of sedentary, sit-and-wait foraging strategists. The combination of a low metabolic rate, a long reproductive lifespan, and steady, low-level fecundity positions this species firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical anurans, prioritizing adult survival and repeated breeding opportunities over a single, explosive reproductive event.
